opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's made me think about it a lot, and my feelings are a bit mixed.

On one hand, DeepSeek was really encouraging. It showed that you don't necessarily need the absolute largest compute budget in the world to do frontier work. With R1 especially, a lot of the key ideas were things academia had been talking about for years: reinforcement learning, reasoning, letting the model explore and get feedback from verifiable rewards. They were relatively simple ideas, executed extremely well and with great engineering discipline. And they open-sourced it. For someone like me who has worked on RL for a long time, that was exciting. It said the algorithmic insight still matters, and a relatively small, focused team can push the frontier.

On the other hand, Operator, and agents more broadly, reminded me how big the gap has become in some areas. To build a good agent product you need a strong base model, huge amounts of interaction data, infrastructure to run thousands of environments in parallel, and a product loop with real users. A university lab simply doesn't have most of that. If academia tries to compete head-on, training the biggest model or shipping the best agent, I think we'll lose. That's just the reality.

So my view has shifted toward this: academia shouldn't try to be a smaller version of an industry lab. It should do the things industry is structurally less likely to do. Explore riskier ideas that may not pay off for three to five years. Study the science of why these methods work, like why RL on reasoning generalizes, or when it collapses. Build open frameworks, benchmarks, and environments the whole community can use. In our own work on open RL training systems, a big part of the motivation is exactly that: if the infrastructure is open and efficient, many more people can do meaningful experiments instead of only a few companies.

And there's another thing people underestimate: talent. Many of the people doing the most important work at DeepSeek and elsewhere are very young, often fresh out of school or still students. Universities are still where those people are trained and where they get the freedom to think differently. That role doesn't go away.

So I'm not pessimistic. Academia's place hasn't disappeared, but it's changed. We have to be more honest about what we can't do, and much more deliberate about what only we can do.

fable-5.1.text:
The honest answer is that both releases made me more comfortable with where academia sits, not less. Let me explain, because on the surface it looks like the opposite should be true.

DeepSeek is the clearer case. What they showed with R1 is that a relatively small team, with far fewer GPUs than the top American labs, could reproduce frontier reasoning capability and publish how they did it. For people like me, that was genuinely encouraging. For a couple of years, the narrative was that the only things that matter are compute and data, and if you don't have tens of thousands of H100s you should go home. DeepSeek's work pushed back on that. A lot of their gains came from algorithmic choices, from training recipes, from being clever about reinforcement learning on top of a base model. Those are exactly the kinds of questions a university group can study. We can't train the base model, but we can study how to turn a base model into a reasoner, and we can do it in the open.

Operator is a different lesson. It's a product, and it depends on infrastructure, safety work, and integration that no lab is going to build. But if you look underneath it, the core problem is agents: how does a model perceive an environment, plan over many steps, recover from mistakes, and know when to ask a human. Those are research questions that are far from solved. Operator is impressive precisely because it works in a narrow band of situations, and it fails in interesting ways outside of that band. Understanding why, and building the benchmarks and training methods to fix it, is work that academia is well suited for.

So my view has shifted in this sense. I used to think the right thing for academic groups was to stay away from anything that looked like competing with the labs. Now I think we should be more ambitious, but in a specific direction. We shouldn't compete on scale. We should compete on understanding. Take an open model, run a careful RL experiment, write down exactly what happened, and release everything. The labs have a hard time doing that, because for them the recipe is the product. For us, the recipe is the paper.

The other change is that I've become more willing to let students work on these "hot" problems. A year ago I worried that if a student spent six months on reasoning or agents, a company would release something that made the whole project moot. That's still a risk. But DeepSeek showed that the open community can set the agenda sometimes, not only follow it. And I'd rather have students in the arena with that mindset than off to the side waiting for the field to calm down, because it isn't going to.

astra-6.text:
I think these releases make the question sharper: where can academia make a distinctive contribution? DeepSeek raises questions about how much progress comes from resources and how much comes from finding better methods. Operator points toward systems that take actions, rather than simply generate answers. That opens up research questions about learning, planning, and evaluating whether an agent can reliably complete a task.

For academia, I don’t think the best response is necessarily to reproduce an industrial product with a smaller budget. We should look for fundamental questions where a new idea or a carefully designed experiment can change how people approach the problem. Why does a method work? Where does it fail? Can we develop principles that generalize beyond one model or one benchmark?

So I see both pressure and opportunity. Industry moves quickly, and that affects which projects make sense for a university lab. But building an impressive system doesn’t mean the underlying scientific questions are settled. Academia has an important role in identifying and pursuing those questions, as well as training people who can ask the next ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they make the question of academia’s role more urgent. When you see something like DeepSeek, it challenges the assumption that progress is simply a matter of having the largest budget. There is still room for better algorithms, better training methods, and more efficient use of compute. Those are areas where academic research can contribute.

Operator raises a slightly different question: how do we move from a model that gives you an answer to a system that can actually do something? Once an agent interacts with an environment, it has to handle uncertainty, recover from mistakes, and understand whether it has completed the task. That creates a lot of research questions beyond improving a language model’s benchmark score.

So I wouldn’t frame academia’s goal as reproducing everything a leading company does. We should ask which important questions aren’t being answered, and where a small team can develop an idea that changes how people approach the problem. We also have a responsibility to study these systems openly and train students who can question the assumptions behind them.
